title: The Challenger Sale
subtitle: Teach prospects something they don't know then lead them to your solution
useWhen: You're selling to prospects who say they're satisfied with how things are. You're in competitive situations where all vendors look similar. Relationship-building alone isn't winning deals anymore.
howToUse: Based on a five-year study of 6,000 sales professionals by Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson, The Challenger Sale found that the highest-performing reps don't just build relationships, they challenge the customer's thinking. The Challenger approach has three moves: Teach (share a provocative insight the prospect hasn't considered), Tailor (connect the insight to the specific business or individual), Take Control (guide the conversation toward your unique solution confidently). The insight you teach must be counterintuitive and directly connected to a problem only you solve.
steps: Build your Challenger insight before any sales conversation, use the prompt below.
The insight must be specific to the prospect's industry and genuinely surprising.
Teach the insight first before connecting it to your product sequence matters.

Practice delivering the insight in under 90 seconds without sounding like a pitch. The insight you teach must be something the prospect genuinely didn't know — not something they agree with immediately. If they nod too fast, you haven't challenged them. The best Challenger insights make the prospect slightly uncomfortable. That discomfort is the opening. PRO TIP
origin: Matthew Dixon & Brent Adamson, The Challenger Sale, 2011
promptBody:
I PROMPT — COPY & PASTE READY
Act as a Challenger Sale strategist.
My product: [WHAT YOU SELL AND THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES]
Prospect type: [INDUSTRY, ROLE, COMPANY STAGE]
Common assumption: [WHAT THEY CURRENTLY BELIEVE OR DO THAT YOUR
PRODUCT CHALLENGES]
Build a full Challenger approach:
TEACH: What counterintuitive insight about their industry or business would genuinely
surprise them?
(must be specific, data-backed, and relevant)
TAILOR: How does this insight connect specifically to their role, their pain, or their goals?
TAKE CONTROL: How do I guide from the insight to the conversation about my solution
— naturally,
without feeling like a pivot?
Write the opening 3–4 sentences I would say out loud.
Also write the Take Control transition — the bridge from the insight to my solution in 1–2
sentences.
